recentItems.title: Art Works: Artist Jeremy Leatinu‘u explores different mediums for telling our shared stories
recentItems.description:
Multidisciplinary artist Jeremy Leatinu‘u spoke with Auckland Art Gallery for our Art Works series, where we chat with artists to explore questions such as: What is art? Who is it for? And, why should we care about it?  

Leatinu‘u talks about how we don’t always find our own meaning within an artwork until after we’ve left it. Watch the full video below.
___

Jeremy Leatinu‘u (Ngāti Maniapoto, Sāmoa) describes his artistic practice with one word: haututū. This kupu is often used to refer to child-like cheekiness, curiosity or propensity for mischief. But here, Leatinu‘u describes haututū as ‘someone that likes to try different things. Someone that is interested in exploring stories’.  

He says, ‘I’ve worked in sculpture, performance art, video and film. There have been a few different mediums that I’ve been interested in working in. And I think that’s kind of part of the haututū aspect that I enjoy.’  

Watch the full video for more, including why monuments are so interesting to Leatinu‘u and how art shapes the stories we tell and the stories we leave behind when we’re gone. 

See more stories from Auckland Art Gallery: https://www.aucklandartgallery.com/explore/stories-and-voices

recentItems.title: Art Works: Abstract painter Judy Millar on the importance of keeping our imaginations open
recentItems.description:
Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki presents Art Works, a series where we chat with artists to explore questions such as: What is art? Who is it for? And, why should we care about it? In this installment, painter Judy Millar talks about how art can be scary for people, and what lies beyond our fear. 

------

‘Art can be so scary for people,’ says painter Judy Millar, who lives and works in Tāmaki Makarau Auckland. ‘That’s partly art’s fault,’ she continues, ‘because art sets itself so high. And yet, as children, we all participate in art.’ 

Millar is known for her large-scale and abstract paintings. However, in this kōrero, she says, ‘In terms of abstract paintings, I really am pushing against it. I’m taking bits of it up and I’m rejecting a lot of it as well. I don’t want to be separated from our real-world experience.’ 

‘There may not be an instantly recognisable image or an instantly recognisable story,’ she continues, ‘but I want it to be very much located in that real-world experience.’ 

Instead of moving on quickly from art that might feel intimidating or scary at first, Millar invites us to take our time. ‘If you spend some time with it, I think you begin to recognise things.’ 

Watch the full video for more on what Millar is working on now, keeping our imaginations open, and how art can be dangerous. 

See more stories from Auckland Art Gallery: https://www.aucklandartgallery.com/explore/stories-and-voices

recentItems.title: The Art of: Making Something Your Own
recentItems.description:
Artist Lu Pingyuan from Forever Tomorrow: Chinese Art Now and Shane Liu, owner of beloved Auckland restaurant Sumthin' Dumplin' sit down to chat about how food, art and cultural tradition shape our identities.

Walk into Sumthin' Dumplin' on Auckland’s Lorne Street and you'll get the sense straight away that while the food may be rooted in Chinese tradition, the brand tells a broader story. There are traces of family history, hip-hop culture, Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland, and the Māori and Pacific communities that have shaped founder Shane Liu's life. 

'When I designed Sumthin' Dumplin', I based it on my identity,' Shane explains.

When artist Lu Pingyuan visited the restaurant during his time in Auckland, he noticed the same thing. 

'I sensed the coalescence of many cultures the moment I stepped into this store, ' he says. 

That observation becomes the starting point for a conversation that stretches well beyond food. It opens bigger questions about creativity, influence and what it means to inherit a culture while also reshaping it. For both Shane and Pingyuan, creativity isn't about preserving tradition exactly as it was handed down, but about transforming it into something personal. 

Read more: https://www.aucklandartgallery.com/explore/stories-and-voices/the-art-of-making-something-your-own

Explore Forever Tomorrow at Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki: https://www.aucklandartgallery.com/visit/exhibitions/forever-tomorrow-chinese-art-now

Discover Sumthin' Dumplin': https://www.aucklandnz.com/explore/sumthin-dumplin-lorne-street

recentItems.title: Pat Hanly Creativity Project and Awards 2025 | Wrap-up
recentItems.description:
In this video, we wrap up the 23nd edition from 2025. The journey of this collaborative project begins with school visits to the Gallery, where over 800 students from twenty-eight secondary schools gather inspiration through engaging with exhibitions and participating in artist-led workshops. They then return to their classrooms to develop their own artworks in response to a theme. This year’s theme was Ko Wai Au?/ Who Am I? 

The artworks in this year’s student exhibition represent a selection of top student submissions chosen by Gallery staff that demonstrate outstanding creativity, originality and skill. Displayed within the Gallery, these young artists’ works are placed in conversation with our other exhibitions and taonga (treasures), creating a tangible link between generations of artists from Aotearoa. 

The opening of the exhibition was celebrated with a Young Gallery Night: a special evening with music, drop-in workshops, a fashion show by students from Fashion + Sustainability Whitecliffe, dance performances by students from Dance Studies University of Auckland, screen printing and zine making workshops by students from AUT, video artworks presented from Elam School of Arts,  and performances from Auckland Philharmonia as part of their Aspiring Musicians programme. 

Participating schools: Albany Senior High School, Aorere College, Auckland Grammar School, Birkenhead College, Dilworth School, Elim Christian College Mt Albert, Glendowie College, Henderson High School, Howick College, James Cook High School, Macleans College, Mahurangi College, Marist College, Michael Park School, Mount Albert Grammar School, Papakura High School, Papatoetoe High School, Pinehurst School, Pukekohe High School, Rangitoto College, Saint Kentigern College, Southern Cross Campus, St Cuthbert’s College, St Dominic’s Catholic College, St Peter’s College, Tangaroa College, Titirangi Rudolf Steiner School and Waitakere College. 

Special thanks to artist Ani O’Neill and the Hanly family for their continued support of this initiative to stimulate creativity. This project was made possible with the generous support of the Friedlander Foundation, The Sir William, Lady Lois Manchester Charitable Trust and Gordon Harris. This project is Enriching Local Curriculum (ELC) based and supported by the Ministry of Education.

recentItems.title: HĪKOI – A Taane Mete Performance
recentItems.description:
This video showcases the 2025 Matariki performance by Taane Mete at Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki – HĪKOI.
 
Taane is joined by Milly Grant-Koria, Tiaki Kerei, Celeste Botha, Jasmin Canuel and Lorelle McNaughton 
 
Dance, waiata, live music and poetry constellate in this performance, inspired by the star Tupuārangi and the peaceful protest hīkoi (march) of November 2024. In HĪKOI the nine stars of Matariki and the nine-day march intertwine, symbolising solidarity and the cosmic wellspring of relationships between atua (gods), people, place, space, time and purpose.
 
HĪKOI – A Taane Mete Performance is proudly supported by Auckland Council and the city centre targeted rate.
 
Cast:
 
Taane Mete, Principal dancer and choreographer, vocalist
Milly Grant-Koria, Vocalist
Tiaki Kerei ,Dancer
Celeste Botha, Dancer
Jasmin Canuel, Dancer
Lorelle McNaughton, Pianist
Josh Clark, Composer
Rosemary Whitehead, Costume designer
Ngaronoa Renata, Mystic poet

recentItems.title: Te pūrākau o Matariki | The story of Matariki
recentItems.description:
Mānawatia a Matariki!

Ko te mahutatanga o Matariki ki te rangi e tohu ana i te tau hou Māori – He wā hokinga mahara, he wā whakahou, he wā whakanui anō hoki.

He pūrākau, he kōrero kei tēnā, kei tēnā o ngā whetū e iwa o Matariki. Mātakihia tēnei kiriata kia ako ai i ngā whetū me te whakamāramatanga o Matariki.

Tēnā, haria mai tō whānau ki te whare toi, ka piri mai ai ki a mātou ki te whakanui i a Matariki ā te 20 o Paraire. Tirohia te whānuitanga o ngā taipitopito ki konei: www.aucklandartgallery.com/Matariki2025

E wātea ana ngā tapanga reo Māori, reo Ingarihi hoki mā te pāwhiri ki te pātene Ngā Tautuhinga me te kōwhiri i te kōwhiringa reo ki te wāhanga Kupu Hauraro/CC.  

Mānawatia a Matariki! 

The appearance of Matariki in the sky signals the Māori New Year – a time of reflection, renewal and celebration.

Each of the nine stars within the Matariki cluster tells a different story. Watch this video to learn more about the stars and the meaning of Matariki.

Then, bring your whānau to the Gallery and join us in celebrating Matariki on Friday 20 June. More info on our website here: www.aucklandartgallery.com/Matariki2025

Te reo Māori and English captions are available by clicking the Settings button and selecting the language option in the Subtitles/CC section.

recentItems.title: Kia whakahou, kia whakaora | Project update
recentItems.description:
The Gallery is replacing the roof of its 135-year-old heritage building, essential work that will help protect the beautiful old building and precious artworks within for future generations.  

The heritage restoration project is called ‘Kia whakahou, kia whakaora’, which means to ‘restore’ or ‘heal’ in te reo Māori.  

Here, Paul Tyler, General Manager of Property at Tātaki Auckland Unlimited gives us a behind-the-scenes tour and update on the current status of the project, which began in February 2023.

You can find more information on Kia whakahou, kia whakaora on our website here: www.aucklandartgallery.com/visit/visitor-information/heritage-restoration-project-kia-whakahou-kia-whakaora

recentItems.title: Pat Hanly Creativity Project and Awards 2024 | Wrap-up
recentItems.description:
Held annually, the Pat Hanly Creativity Awards acknowledge Pat Hanly’s outstanding contribution to New Zealand contemporary art and his passion for art education and supporting young artists. The awards also highlight the crucial role of art education in shaping future creatives and helping them connect with the wider art community. 

In this video, we wrap up the 22nd edition from 2024. This year, the awards have evolved into a collaborative project. The journey begins with school visits to the Gallery, where over 500 students from thirteen schools gather inspiration through engaging with exhibitions and participating in artist-led workshops. They then return to their classrooms to develop their own artworks in response to a theme. This year’s theme was Tōku Tūrangawaewae – my place to stand. Tūrangawaewae is a place of ancestral connections and empowerment, a place one can call home. 

The artworks in the inaugural student exhibition represent a selection of top student submissions chosen by Gallery staff that demonstrate outstanding creativity, originality and skill. Displayed within the Gallery, these young artists’ works are placed in conversation with our other exhibitions and taonga or treasures, creating a tangible link between generations of artists from Aotearoa. 

The opening of the exhibition was celebrated with a Young Gallery Night: a special evening with music, drop-in workshops, a fashion show by students from Fashion + Sustainability Whitecliffe, dance performances by students from Dance Studies University of Auckland and a harakeke weaving workshop by students from Elam School of Arts, spoken word, and many many more things. 

Participating schools: Birkenhead College, Henderson High School, James Cook High School, Macleans College, Marist College, Michael Park School, Papatoetoe High School, Pinehurst School, St Cuthbert’s College, St Dominic’s Catholic College, Southern Cross Campus, Tangaroa College and Waiheke High School. 

Special thanks to the Hanly family for their continued support of this initiative to stimulate creativity. This project was made possible with the generous support of the Friedlander Foundation, The Sir William, Lady Lois Manchester Charitable Trust and Gordon Harris. This project is Enriching Local Curriculum (ELC) based and supported by the Ministry of Education.
